title: Working in a Startup, Where Ambiguity Is the Job
summary: A startup is still searching for its business. What that means day to day: many hats, decisions you can undo, tech debt you choose, and writing things down in time.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Your first week at a startup, the founder drops a goal in Slack: "We need to cut churn." No spec, no ticket, no PM. By Thursday you've read a pile of support emails, sat in on two customer calls and shipped a tiny change to the onboarding email. Nobody asked for that exact change. Nobody told you not to, either.

If that sounds fun, you'll probably enjoy startup life. If it sounds stressful, that's fair, and better to know before you sign. This post covers both sides: the ownership and speed people join for, and the ambiguity, debt and whiplash that grow from the same root. It's the startup chapter of the series that opened with big corp vs startup vs outsourcing.

A quick word on where I'm coming from. My first job, in 2018, was as a fresher front-end developer on the founding team of Propman Guru, a real-estate startup. There was barely any process, and I learned to ship by shipping. Later I spent almost four years at PrimeData, a B2B startup building a customer data platform, and today I'm a part-time co-founder at BonBon Mobility. Different stages, but most of what felt strange had the same cause.

The one fact behind everything

Steve Blank defines a startup as "an organization formed to search for a repeatable and scalable business model" (What's A Startup? First Principles). The word that matters is search. A big company already knows what it sells and to whom, so its job is to do that reliably at scale. A startup is still guessing, and every feature it ships is partly an experiment to check the guess.

Speed of learning > polish

Before a startup finds something customers will pay for, the most useful thing you ship is information. A rough version that shows by Friday that nobody wants the feature beats a polished one that shows the same thing three months later. Once you see learning as the product, a lot of startup decisions stop looking sloppy.

Paul Graham makes a related point in Do Things That Don't Scale: early on, founders recruit users by hand and do work that would look odd at a big company. One example from the essay is what Y Combinator calls the "Collison installation." When someone agreed to try Stripe, the founders would say "Right then, give me your laptop" and set it up on the spot. That's the startup trade in one gesture. You skip the clean, repeatable way because right now speed and direct contact teach you more.

So healthy startups put up with things that would make a big company wince: skipping process, cutting scope, shipping the rough version, deleting last month's code. That's fine when it buys learning. When it's just noise, it's a failure mode, and we'll get to those.

Wearing many hats

In a big company you own a deep, narrow slice and lean on specialists for everything else. A startup flips that. In a single week you might:

  • Build an API endpoint in the morning and fix a CSS bug in the afternoon.
  • Set up the deploy pipeline because nobody else has.
  • Join a call with an annoyed customer and file their bug as tomorrow's ticket.
  • Give your view on pricing, a hire, or which feature to drop.

You own outcomes more than tickets. The upside is range and fast feedback: your work reaches customers within days, and you can see what it did. The cost is that you're often a little outside your expertise, in a codebase only one or two people fully understand. Being comfortable with "I'll figure it out" is most of the startup temperament. If you need to be the expert before you act, the first months will hurt.

It also helps to know which hats don't fit yet. A good startup engineer says, "I set up CI, but I'm not sure about the security config. Can someone sanity-check it?" Wearing many hats is normal. Pretending they all fit is how things break without anyone noticing.

Ambiguity is the job

New startup engineers often wait to be told what to do, the way school and big companies trained them, and then feel lost when nobody does. Nobody is neglecting you. The team doesn't know the answer yet, and helping find it is part of why they hired you.

In practice that looks like this:

  • Define your own scope. Take a fuzzy goal like "cut churn," find a piece you can ship this week, and propose it before anyone writes a spec.
  • Sort decisions by how hard they are to undo. In his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders, Jeff Bezos called the "consequential and irreversible or nearly irreversible" ones one-way doors. Most decisions, he wrote, are two-way doors, and those "can and should be made quickly by high judgment individuals or small groups." Picking a charting library or rewording the pricing page? Decide today. Choosing where customer money lives or signing a three-year contract? Slow down.
  • Ask "what's the cheapest way to learn this?" before "what's the right way to build this?" Sometimes the answer is a spreadsheet and a phone call.

Bezos's worry in that letter was big companies running every decision through the heavy one-way-door process, which leads to "slowness, unthoughtful risk aversion, failure to experiment sufficiently." Startups face the opposite risk. In a footnote he adds that companies which habitually make one-way-door calls the light, fast way "go extinct before they get large."

What good looks like

The startup engineers people trust most rarely ask "what should I work on?" They show up with "here's what I think we're missing, here's the cheap version I'd ship to test it, and here's why." Do that every week and people start handing you the bigger calls.

Debt you choose, debt that happens to you

A startup needs speed, and it also needs to survive its own code. Martin Fowler's Technical Debt Quadrant is a handy way to think about the tension. He sorts debt along two axes, deliberate or inadvertent and prudent or reckless, and argues that "the useful distinction isn't between debt or non-debt, but between prudent and reckless debt." Prudent debt buys you something, like an earlier release, and its interest stays manageable.

Here's how that plays out in a startup codebase:

Kind of debtVerdictWhy
Deliberate and visible ("hardcode it now, generalize if it works")HealthyYou bought speed on purpose, and there's a note saying where to pay it back.
Accidental and untracked (mess nobody decided on)DangerousIt grows until shipping anything takes a week. A startup can find customers and still stall here.
Debt in the core (what survives every pivot: auth, billing, the data model)Pay down earlyCode you'll keep for years deserves real care.
Debt in experiments (probably deleted next month)Accept itPolishing code you're about to throw away is the actual waste.

Fowler also notes that prudent debt taken to reach a release "may not be worth paying down if the interest payments are sufficiently small." So the real skill is judging which code is core and which is disposable. Miss one way and you gold-plate experiments nobody will keep. Miss the other way and the core rots until every change feels risky.

Write things down before the team doubles

Small teams run on fast, low-ceremony talk. You turn around and ask, decisions happen over lunch, and standup is a Slack thread. At five people that works well. Its weak spot stays hidden until it hurts: knowledge that lives only in heads and DMs.

The math gets unfriendly fast. Fred Brooks pointed out in The Mythical Man-Month (1975) that communication overhead climbs quickly as people join a project (Brooks's law). Count the pairs: five people have 10 possible one-to-one conversations, ten people have 45, and fifty have 1,225. Asking around can't keep up with that. As the team grows, the one person who knows why the payment retry works the way it does is too busy to explain it a fifth time.

You don't need big-company documentation. You need a handful of things written down before the pain arrives: the big decisions and why you made them, how to run and deploy the system, and how the main pieces fit together. A short decision log is a good start (here's one busy teams actually keep).

The small-to-mid transition

Somewhere between a handful of people and a hundred, the habits that made the startup fast start to creak, and process (the thing many people joined to get away from) comes back. Nobody betrayed the culture. Coordination that cost nothing at five people costs real effort at fifty, and somebody has to pay for it.

What changesEarly startupScaling (mid-size)
DecisionsAnyone, right awayMore people affected, so a bit of alignment first
ProcessBarely anyLightweight sprints, on-call, required reviews
RolesEveryone does everythingFirst dedicated infra, QA or PM hires
KnowledgeIn a few headsWritten down, or lost

Some process also arrives from outside. At BonBon, our Mini App runs inside the VETC app, so our work went through the partner's OWASP security review, an independent pentest and their change approval. That's the price of being trusted with someone else's users, and it's worth paying. Partners, enterprise customers and investors each bring a bar of their own.

Some early engineers hate this phase and leave for the next tiny startup. Others grow into the people who design the lightweight structure. Both are fine choices. Knowing the shift is coming lets you pick one on purpose, instead of feeling like the company you joined has vanished. And if you find you like the structure more than you resent it, a bigger company might suit you well.

Failure modes to watch for

Failure modeWhat it looks likeWhat helps
BurnoutCrunch is the normal state, and late nights are expectedTreat a sustainable pace as a feature. Constant crunch is a warning sign, and nobody should wear it as a badge.
Hero cultureOne person holds everything together; the bus factor is oneSpread knowledge, write down the critical paths, and pair on the scary parts.
Priority whiplashMonday's top priority is forgotten by FridayAsk for a short written focus for the week or month, and say out loud what each switch will cost.
Chaos that looks like speedLots of activity, little shipped or learnedTie each piece of work to a guess you're testing and a number you'll check.
Equity dazzleTaking a deep pay cut for options you don't understandTreat equity as a maybe. Ask about vesting, the strike price and how long you'd have to exercise if you left.

How to grow in a startup

  • Optimize for learning speed, yours and the company's. Ship the cheap test, and count the skills you pick up as part of the pay.
  • Bring problems and proposed bets along with finished tickets. Initiative is what people remember.
  • Be deliberate about debt: accept it in experiments, protect the core. That judgment is what earns you bigger decisions.
  • Write down just enough that your work still makes sense after the team doubles.
  • When the scaling phase comes, help design the lightweight process. The people who shape it usually end up leading it.

Career growth in a startup is fast and fuzzy. Titles can inflate, scope can land on you overnight, and there's rarely a calibrated ladder. In return, your impact is visible, and sitting close to the business can give you leadership experience earlier than a big company would. If you'd like breadth without betting your week on one product's survival, outsourcing offers a different trade.

Try this week

  • Pick one fuzzy goal on your team and write a one-paragraph proposal for the cheapest test you could ship by Friday.
  • Before your next decision, ask: one-way door or two-way door? If it's two-way, decide today.
  • Label one shortcut you took on purpose as debt in your tracker, with a line on when you'll pay it back.
  • Write down one decision that currently lives only in someone's head.
  • If you're weighing an offer, ask about vesting and the exercise window before you compare salaries.

faqs.q: What's the biggest shift when moving from a big company to a startup?
faqs.a: Treating ambiguity as part of the job. In a big company someone usually decides what matters before a ticket reaches you. In a startup nobody knows yet, so you carve a shippable piece out of a fuzzy goal, decide reversible things quickly and ask what the cheapest way to learn is. The second shift is caring more about what you learn this week than about how polished the output looks.

faqs.q: Is it normal to feel out of my depth in a startup?
faqs.a: Yes. A small team means one person covers backend, frontend, deploys and customer calls in the same week, often on code only one or two people fully understand. Say which parts you're unsure about and ask for a second pair of eyes. That's normal in a startup, and much safer than pretending every hat fits.

faqs.q: How should a startup handle technical debt?
faqs.a: On purpose. Martin Fowler's Technical Debt Quadrant separates prudent debt, taken knowingly to buy something like an earlier release, from reckless debt. Take visible, deliberate shortcuts in experiments that may be deleted, pay down debt early in the core that survives every pivot (auth, billing, the data model) and don't let untracked mess pile up.

faqs.q: Why do startups add process as they grow?
faqs.a: Because coordination gets expensive. Five people have 10 possible one-to-one pairs and fifty people have 1,225, so asking around stops working. Decisions need a bit of alignment, knowledge has to be written down and specialist roles appear. Partners and enterprise customers also bring their own security and approval requirements.

faqs.q: Should I join a startup for the equity?
faqs.a: Treat equity as a maybe and make sure the salary works on its own. Options can end up worth nothing if the company never has an exit. Ask about vesting, the strike price and how long you'd have to exercise after leaving. The role, the ownership and what you'll learn are steadier reasons to join.
